p.src:
Galilean transformations cannot make the speed of light the same in every inertial frame. The corrected relations are, first in $c=1$ units, $\begin{aligned}x'&=\frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}, &
t'&=\frac{t-vx}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}.
\end{aligned}$ Restoring ordinary units gives $\begin{aligned}x'&=\frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}, &
t'&=\frac{t-vx/c^2}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}.
\end{aligned}$

There are three cases: $\begin{aligned}\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2 &>0 &&\text{timelike},\\

p.src: If the astronaut begins at rest and accelerates, the description changes between a succession of instantaneous inertial frames. The same statement applies to a realistic twin who launches, turns, and decelerates rather than being born at cruising speed.

p.src: Response: It is not necessary to begin with the slogan that time is a fourth dimension. The Lorentz transformation itself forces space and time to mix, while the interval $t^2-x^2-y^2-z^2$ treats them as parts of one geometry with a different sign for time and space. At low velocity the mixing becomes negligible and familiar Newtonian intuition returns. At relativistic velocity, however, space and time cannot be regarded as fundamentally decoupled.
